description: Kosher dietary laws, Brit Milah, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, marriage and burial rites.
content_html:
Dietary Laws: Kosher and Terefah

Jewish dietary laws are called kashrut. Food that meets these laws is Kosher (permitted), while food that does not meet them is Terefah (forbidden). The main laws are set out in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14. These laws define which animals may be eaten, how they must be slaughtered and prepared, and how different food types must be kept apart.

Permitted land animals must have split hooves and chew the cud — so cattle, sheep and deer are kosher, while pigs are not (they have split hooves but do not chew the cud). Permitted fish must have fins and scales — so salmon and trout are kosher, while shellfish and eels are not. Birds of prey are forbidden; domestic birds such as chicken and turkey are permitted. All insects are prohibited.

Key Fact

The biblical prohibition “do not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Deuteronomy 14:21) led to a complete separation of meat and milk. Kosher households maintain two sets of crockery, cutlery and cooking utensils. A waiting period (between one and six hours depending on tradition) must pass before eating dairy after meat. Pareve foods — neither meat nor dairy, such as fish, eggs, fruit and vegetables — may be eaten with either.

To be kosher, animals must be slaughtered by a trained shochet (ritual slaughterer) using a single, swift cut to the throat with a perfectly smooth blade. This minimises suffering and ensures rapid blood loss. The blood must then be drained through salting or broiling, because Leviticus 7:26–27 forbids consuming blood. The impact of dietary laws on Jewish life is significant: observant Jews can only eat in restaurants with kosher certification, must check food labels carefully and may face challenges when travelling or in non-Jewish social settings.

Orthodox Jews follow the laws of kashrut strictly as a binding commandment, maintaining two sets of kitchen equipment and buying only kosher-certified produce. They see dietary law as a discipline that sanctifies daily life and connects them to the covenant at Sinai.

Many Reform Jews do not observe the dietary laws in the same way. Some keep the broad biblical categories (avoiding pork and shellfish) but do not separate meat and milk. Others do not observe kashrut at all, arguing that the spiritual and ethical dimensions of Judaism matter more than ancient food regulations. Progressive Judaism emphasises the underlying values — such as reducing animal suffering — rather than legal detail.

Rites of Passage: Birth

Jewish rites of passage connect the individual to the covenant, the community and the tradition. When a baby girl is born, she is formally welcomed in a synagogue naming ceremony, often called Simchat Bat or Zeved HaBat in Sephardic tradition. The father is called to the Torah and a prayer is recited for the health of mother and child.

For a baby boy, Brit Milah (the covenant of circumcision) takes place on the eighth day. This links directly to the covenant with Abraham in Genesis 17:9–12, where G‑d commanded that all male descendants be circumcised as a sign of the covenant. The ceremony is performed by a trained Mohel. The baby is placed on a ceremonial chair called the Chair of Elijah (the prophet Elijah is said to be present at every circumcision). The Sandek — typically a respected elder or grandfather — holds the infant during the procedure. The baby’s Hebrew name is then announced for the first time.

Bar and Bat Mitzvah

At 13 for boys and 12 for girls, Jewish young people reach religious adulthood. A boy becomes a Bar Mitzvah (son of the commandment) and a girl becomes a Bat Mitzvah (daughter of the commandment). From this point they are personally responsible for fulfilling the Mitzvot — the father’s prayer at the ceremony traditionally thanks G‑d for releasing him from responsibility for his child’s transgressions.

Preparation involves months of study, learning to read Hebrew and to chant the Torah portion assigned for that Shabbat. At the Bar Mitzvah service, the young man reads from the Sefer Torah on the Bimah in front of the congregation, often giving a short speech about his portion. A celebration meal (kiddush) follows. Bat Mitzvah ceremonies vary: in Reform and Liberal communities, girls read from the Torah just as boys do; in Orthodox communities the ceremony may take the form of a separate Bat Chayil ceremony, where the girl gives a talk but does not read from the Torah during the main service.

Key Fact

The key difference between Orthodox and Reform practice at a girl’s coming of age: Reform Judaism celebrates Bat Mitzvah with full Torah reading in the main service, treating boys and girls equally. Orthodox communities may hold a Bat Chayil (“daughter of valour”) ceremony instead — a significant event but separate from the male Torah-reading service.

Jewish Marriage: Kiddushin

Jewish marriage is called Kiddushin, from the Hebrew root meaning “holiness.” The marriage takes place under the Huppah (wedding canopy), which symbolises the new home the couple will build together. Before the ceremony, a Ketubah (marriage contract) is signed, specifying the husband’s obligations to his wife. Seven blessings (Sheva Brachot) are recited, connecting the wedding to the creation of humanity in Genesis.

The groom places a plain gold ring on the bride’s right index finger, declaring “You are consecrated to me with this ring according to the law of Moses and Israel.” The ceremony concludes with the groom breaking a glass underfoot — traditionally interpreted as recalling the destruction of the Temple, so that joy is never complete without remembering communal loss. Genesis 2:24 provides the scriptural foundation for marriage: “That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.”

Judaism insists on burial rather than cremation, out of respect for the body created in G‑d’s image (Genesis 1:27) and in anticipation of bodily resurrection. The body is washed and purified (tahara) by volunteers (chevra kadisha) and dressed in simple white linen shrouds (tachrichim) to emphasise equality in death. Burial takes place as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

As a sign of grief, mourners perform Kriah — the tearing of a garment. A seven-day mourning period called shiva follows, during which the bereaved remain at home, mirrors are covered and the community comes to offer comfort. The Kaddish prayer is recited by mourners at the graveside and during services for eleven months after death. Significantly, the Kaddish contains no mention of death or grief — it is purely praise of G‑d, affirming faith even in loss.
exam_tip_html: For questions on dietary laws, be precise: state the source (Leviticus 11 or Deuteronomy 14:21), the rule (e.g. separation of meat and milk) and the impact on daily life. On rites of passage questions, a very common error is mixing up the roles of the Mohel and the Sandek at Brit Milah — the Mohel performs the circumcision; the Sandek holds the baby. For Bar/Bat Mitzvah, always note the difference between Reform (Bat Mitzvah with Torah reading) and Orthodox (Bat Chayil) to show awareness of divergent emphases. The 15-mark Discuss may ask whether dietary laws or Shabbat is more important to Jewish identity — use Leviticus 11 and Genesis 17:9–12 as your anchoring sources. Correct spelling of “Kiddushin,” “Huppah,” “Ketubah” and “Brit Milah” is rewarded on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kosher laws (Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy 14) define permitted animals, humane slaughter and the complete separation of meat and milk; Orthodox Jews follow these strictly while some Reform Jews observe only the broader biblical categories or none at all.
  • Key rites of passage connect Jews to the covenant and community: Brit Milah (eighth day, Mohel and Sandek) marks entry into the Abrahamic covenant; Bar/Bat Mitzvah (13/12) marks religious adulthood; Bat Chayil is used in some Orthodox communities instead of a full Torah-reading Bat Mitzvah.
  • Jewish marriage (Kiddushin) takes place under the Huppah with a Ketubah and the breaking of a glass; burial rites require swift interment, the tearing of clothing (Kriah), a week of shiva mourning and eleven months of Kaddish — which praises G-d but never mentions death.

practice_questions.text: State the meaning of the term 'Kosher'.
practice_questions.marks: Food that is permitted under Jewish dietary law; fit or proper. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the Mohel at a Brit Milah ceremony.
practice_questions.marks: The Mohel is a trained Jewish professional [1] who performs the ritual circumcision on the eighth day of the baby boy's life [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the key features of a Jewish marriage ceremony.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: the ceremony takes place under the Huppah (wedding canopy) symbolising the couple's new home; a Ketubah (marriage contract) is signed before the ceremony; seven blessings (Sheva Brachot) are recited; the groom places a ring on the bride's finger; the groom breaks a glass at the end to recall the destruction of the Temple. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which attitudes towards Jewish dietary laws differ between Orthodox and Reform Jews.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Orthodox Jews follow all aspects of kashrut as binding commandments derived from Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14: they maintain two sets of kitchen equipment, wait between eating meat and dairy, and buy only certified kosher produce. They see dietary law as a discipline sanctifying daily life.
• Many Reform Jews do not observe the full kashrut laws, arguing that the spiritual and ethical principles of Judaism matter more than ancient food regulations. Some avoid pork and shellfish but do not separate meat and milk. Reform Judaism emphasises underlying values such as reducing animal suffering.
• Both groups agree that the underlying purpose of dietary laws is to cultivate mindfulness and holiness in everyday life, but they interpret how strictly this must be applied today.
[6 marks — 3 marks per difference: 1 for a simple statement, 2 for development, 3 for a relevant source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'Brit Milah is the most important Jewish rite of passage.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Brit Milah is the physical sign of the covenant between G-d and Abraham (Genesis 17:9-12), the foundational relationship of Judaism; without it, a male Jew is considered to have broken the covenant.
• It takes place on the eighth day of life, making it the first religious act performed for a Jewish male — prior even to the child having any conscious identity.
• The presence of the metaphorical Chair of Elijah and the naming of the child make it a decisive moment of entry into Jewish identity and community.

Arguments against:
• Bar Mitzvah arguably marks the more significant moment: the child becomes personally responsible for the Mitzvot and takes on adult religious obligations. It is the moment chosen by the individual, not performed on them as infants.
• Yom Kippur (atonement) and Shabbat affect every Jew every week or year; Brit Milah applies only to males and only once.
• Marriage (Kiddushin) is described as the foundation of Jewish family life; Genesis 2:24 calls the married couple 'one flesh'. Without marriage, Jewish continuity and community life would be impossible.
• Burial and the Kaddish connect Jews to belief in resurrection and G-d's ongoing presence even in death, making them profoundly significant to the entire community.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Genesis 17:9-12, Genesis 2:24, Leviticus, the Mitzvot), comparison of male and female rites of passage, Orthodox vs Reform differences noted, and a justified conclusion identifying which rite is most fundamental and why.
Secure: Clear arguments for and against with relevant sources and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points on both sides but sources limited or not developed; conclusion present but not fully argued.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no use of sources. [15 marks — SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of the Kaddish prayer in Jewish mourning.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any three of: the Kaddish is an Aramaic prayer of praise to G-d, recited by mourners at the graveside and during services for eleven months after bereavement; it does not mention death or grief but focuses entirely on praising G-d, showing faith even in loss; reciting it requires a minyan (quorum of ten) and connects the individual mourner to the wider Jewish community; it affirms the ongoing relationship between G-d and the Jewish people even in times of suffering. [3 marks — 1 mark each]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the Sandek's role at a Brit Milah?
options: To perform the circumcision using a specially prepared blade
To carry the baby from the mother to the ceremony
To hold the baby on their lap during the circumcision
To recite the prayers and announce the baby's name

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following describes a Bat Chayil ceremony?
options: A Reform ceremony in which a girl reads from the Torah on the Bimah alongside boys
An Orthodox coming-of-age ceremony for girls that does not include Torah reading in the main service
The ceremony performed for a baby girl on the eighth day of life
A female equivalent of Brit Milah

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ is the Jewish marriage contract signed before the ceremony, specifying the groom's obligations to the bride.
Food that is forbidden under Jewish dietary law is called _____, from the Hebrew word meaning 'torn'.
Match each rite of passage to its key feature:
right: Circumcision on the eighth day, performed by a Mohel
Reading from the Torah on the Bimah at age 13
Marriage ceremony under the Huppah with a Ketubah

flashcard_questions.q: What is Brit Milah and when does it take place?
flashcard_questions.a: The covenant of circumcision; performed on the eighth day of a Jewish boy's life.

flashcard_questions.a: The Mohel — a trained ritual circumciser.

flashcard_questions.a: An Orthodox coming-of-age ceremony for girls, without Torah reading in the main service.
The wedding canopy under which the Jewish marriage ceremony takes place.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the breaking of the glass at a Jewish wedding represent?
flashcard_questions.a: Remembrance of the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem.

glossary_terms.definition: Food that is permitted under Jewish dietary law; from the Hebrew root meaning 'fit' or 'proper'.
Food that is forbidden under Jewish dietary law; literally 'torn' — originally referring to animals killed by beasts of prey.
Ceremonies marking key transitions in a person's life, such as birth, coming of age, marriage and death.
The ceremony of circumcision performed on Jewish male babies on the eighth day of life, representing entry into the covenant between G-d and Abraham.
A trained Jewish professional who performs the ritual circumcision during Brit Milah.
The person, usually the grandfather, who holds the baby on their lap during Brit Milah as a great honour.
Literally 'son of the commandment'; a Jewish boy who at 13 becomes responsible for observing the Mitzvot and may be called to read from the Torah in synagogue.
Literally 'daughter of the commandment'; a Jewish girl who at 12 becomes responsible for observing the Mitzvot.
A celebration of a girl's religious coming of age used in some Orthodox communities, typically involving a speech and celebration but without reading from the Torah in the main synagogue service.
The Jewish betrothal and marriage ceremony, whose name derives from the Hebrew word for 'holiness', emphasising the sacred nature of the bond.
The wedding canopy under which a Jewish couple stands during the marriage ceremony, symbolising their new shared home.
The Jewish marriage contract specifying the groom's obligations to the bride; a legal document signed before the wedding.
An Aramaic prayer praising G-d's greatness, traditionally recited by mourners at burial and during the mourning period; does not mention death.
The tearing of clothing (or a ribbon) worn by immediate relatives of the deceased as a sign of grief, performed at the funeral or just before.
